The fix loop lets an agent fix the CI review's findings before Joe reads a PR. Each push to a PR gets a review. When the review marks findings "fix", the fixer fixes them and pushes, and the push starts the next review. That goes on for up to three fix rounds (code review design 4). So Joe reads code that's already been reviewed and fixed, and the loop shows how two agents work together through a PR. #76 built the fixer and tried it by hand. This issue runs it in CI.
- [Code review design](https://github.com/nimbusscale/road-trip-agent/blob/main/design/code-review.md), sections 4.6 and 4.7.

- ~~Are cleanups, the findings about reuse, speed, or style that are notes at best (code review design 4.1), saved up for a separate pass now and then, so they're fixed without feeding the next review? (Moved from #71.)~~ Settled 2026-10-22 in chat: no. Nothing is built for it. When Joe wants a cleanup pass, he runs `/simplify` by hand on a branch.

- ~~How can the workflow tell that a review ran, when all its commands were blocked?~~ (Moved from #71, then from #75 on 2026-10-20.) The loop stops on a review that marks nothing "fix", so a review whose commands were all blocked would end the loop and get the "ready for Joe" label. One way: the `claude -p` JSON output lists `permission_denials`, and the workflow could fail the step when it isn't empty. Settled 2026-10-22 in chat: two checks. The reviewer's answer takes the fixer's shape: `status` ("done" or "stopped"), `reason`, always a sentence, and `findings`, empty when stopped. The `review-pr` skill tells it to stop when it can't do a step it needs, such as reading the description, the list of earlier findings, or the diff. The review step fails on "stopped", and shows the reason in the job summary. As a backstop, the step also fails when the answer is "done" with no findings and `permission_denials` isn't empty. None of the last six reviews would have tripped that by mistake.

- ~~How do the fix loop and the reviewer keep track of V1 findings, the ones marked "check"? V1 means the label depends on a fact the reviewer can't check from the repo (review rubric, V1). Joe suggested listing them in the PR description, but DEVELOPMENT.md section 7 keeps that to the task and the "Done when" results. Set aside on 2026-10-20 until the loop runs, to see how the signals between the agents work in practice. (Moved from #75 on 2026-10-20.)~~ Settled 2026-10-22 in chat: by hand. A check's thread stays open. Joe has the fact checked, replies on the thread with a marker from his account, and resolves it. The summary doesn't list checks. Written into code review design 4.2. Revisit if checks get lost among the notes.

- ~~Code review design section 4.8 records each finding's outcome from the first PR our reviewer reviews. That's #83, before the loop exists. Until the loop runs, who records the outcomes, and where: a row per review in section 5, or a file per PR? Raised 2026-10-20 while opening #83.~~ Dropped 2026-10-22 in chat. Each finding's outcome is in its thread's marker, so nothing is written down by hand. The round write-ups moved from code review design section 5 to `research/code-review/review-rounds.md`, which isn't added to anymore. Code review design 4.8 and 4.9 say so.

- ~~Should the review wait for the tests to pass? The "Code review" and "Check and deploy" workflows run in parallel, so a PR with failing tests still gets reviewed, at about $0.75 a run, on code that has to change anyway. In the loop, the fixer would also spend a round on findings while the tests fail. Raised 2026-10-21 in chat, while reviewing #83.~~ Settled 2026-10-22 in chat: no change. The pre-commit hook runs `npm run check`, tests included, and the fixer runs it before it commits, so a failing test rarely reaches a review. Accepted for this project.

- ~~How does the fix job know the fixer stopped early?~~ Settled 2026-10-21 in chat, in #76: the fixer returns JSON, checked with `--json-schema`, and a stop is `"status": "stopped"` with its reason (code review design 4.5).

- ~~How does `claude -p --json-schema` check the fixer's answer? The answer schema is a choice between two shapes, "done" and "stopped". The API refuses that: "input_schema does not support oneOf, allOf, or anyOf at the top level". Without a top-level `"type": "object"`, it refuses it for that instead.~~ One way: make the answer one object, with `status` and the other fields nullable, and let `check-fix.ts` check which fields go with which status. Found 2026-10-22 in #76, while setting up the first replay. A replay runs the fixer by hand on a draft copy of an old PR's review round (#76, step 5). Checked with Claude Code 2.1.308. Settled 2026-10-22 in chat: one flat object, with three keys that are always filled in. `status` is "done" or "stopped". `reason` is always a sentence: why it stopped, or for "done", a summary of the round, which the job prints. `replies` is always a list, and empty when stopped. `commit` is dropped, since code reads the checked-out commit from git, and pushes it when it's a new commit on the PR's head. Each reply's `issue` is renamed `deferredTo`, so it's clear it's the issue a deferred finding goes to. It stays `null` for the other outcomes. `check-fix.ts` checks what the schema can't: a "done" answer has at least one reply, and a "stopped" one has none.

- ~~How does the fix job keep the sandbox's empty files out of the fixer's commit? When the sandbox runs, it makes empty files in the checkout for paths it protects that don't exist yet: `.npmrc`, `.gitmodules`, `yarn.lock`, `pnpm-lock.yaml`, `bunfig.toml`, `.yarnrc`, `.yarnrc.yml`, and six `.env.*` files. `.gitignore` covers none of them, so a fixer that runs `git add -A` would commit them.~~ One way: have the job fail when the fixer's commit adds an empty file, or have the skill name the files it stages. Found 2026-10-22 in #76's first replay, with Claude Code 2.1.308. `CLAUDE_CODE_SUBPROCESS_ENV_SCRUB=1` turns the sandbox on by itself in that version, even with no sandbox settings. Settled 2026-10-22 in chat: add the 13 paths to `.gitignore`. Then `git add -A` skips them, `check-fix.ts`'s check for uncommitted changes doesn't see them, and local sandboxed runs don't show them either. The project uses only npm, and versions are locked, so the list holds.

- ~~How does the fix job keep the fixer from editing the config files in DEVELOPMENT.md section 6?~~ Locally, `.claude/settings.json` has ask rules for them. In CI, Claude Code ignores that file (`.github/workflows/code-review.yml` says why), so the rules don't apply. One way: pass deny rules for those files in the job's `--settings`. Edit rules don't cover a shell command such as `sed`, so the job could also fail when the fixer's commit touches one of them. Raised 2026-10-21 in chat, while reviewing #91. Settled 2026-10-22 in chat: before the fixer starts, the job turns the "ask" rules in `.claude/settings.json` into deny rules, and passes them with `--settings`, along with the sandbox settings. The sandbox mounts each denied file read-only for the fixer's commands, so `sed` and `echo >>` fail too, not only the Edit tool. Tested with Claude Code 2.1.308. Two things the job has to do, found in the test: drop each rule's leading `/`, since in an inline `--settings` string it matches nothing, and expand a wildcard in a file name, such as `tsconfig*.json`, into the exact files, since the sandbox skips those rules. A folder rule, such as `.claude/hooks/**`, works as it is. New disable comments can't be blocked by a file rule, since they go in ordinary code files. So `eslint.config.js` bans them: turn on `@eslint-community/eslint-comments/no-use`, and set `ban-ts-comment`'s `"ts-expect-error"` to `true`. Joe approved that config change 2026-10-22 in chat. There are none in `src/` or `web/` today.

But 4.6 starts a run only on a push, and runs the fix job only when the review marks a finding "fix". A reply isn't a push. A push by Joe gets a review that won't post that finding again, so the fix job is skipped. One way: run the fix job when the review marks a finding "fix", or when a finding that needs attention has a new reply from Joe. Deferred 2026-10-22 from #91's third review ([finding](https://github.com/nimbusscale/road-trip-agent/pull/91#discussion_r4349315316)). Settled 2026-10-22 in chat: the fix job runs when the review marks a finding "fix", or when a finding that needs attention has a reply from Joe after the fixer's. The review job outputs both counts. Joe starts the run by re-running the PR's latest "Code review" run, from the Actions tab or with `gh run rerun <run-id>`. No new trigger. To leave such a finding alone, Joe resolves its thread instead of replying. The cap of three fix rounds still holds.

- ~~How does the fixer edit a skill file, such as `.claude/skills/review-pr/SKILL.md`? With Claude Code 2.1.308, `claude -p` refuses an Edit tool write under `.claude/` unless the permission mode is `bypassPermissions`. An allow rule such as `Edit(.claude/skills/**)`, or `--permission-mode acceptEdits`, doesn't help. Tested 2026-10-22 on #93's PR, #109, where round 1's fixer answered "needs attention" for that reason. Skill files aren't config files (DEVELOPMENT.md section 6), so a fix in one is in the fixer's scope.~~ Settled 2026-10-22 in chat: the fixer doesn't get to edit skill files. A finding whose fix is in one needs attention, and Joe or Claude Code fixes it by hand, as on #109's round 1. Bypassing permissions was turned down, since it would also drop the `--allowedTools` list. Write this into code review design 3.6's list of what needs attention.

- ~~The `fix-pr` skill runs `npx tsx src/code-review/fix-input.ts` and `check-fix.ts`. `npx tsx` fails in Claude Code's sandbox, since the tsx command opens a socket that the sandbox refuses (`listen EPERM`). `node --import tsx <file>` works. Found 2026-10-22 by the first review of #109, which fixed the reviewer's skill.~~ One way: change the `fix-pr` skill the same way, before the fix job runs it in the sandbox. Settled 2026-10-22 in chat, and done in PR #111: the `fix-pr` skill runs both scripts with `node --import tsx`, and code review design 4.5 says so. `npx vitest` works in the sandbox, checked the same day.

- ~~ESLint lints `scratch/`, where the `fix-pr` skill tells the fixer to put throwaway files. On #109, round 1's fixer left `scratch/block-listen.cjs`, and `npm run check` then failed on it. Each CI run starts from a fresh checkout, so this only bites when the fixer leaves a `.js` or `.cjs` file there and then runs the check in the same run.~~ One way: have the skill say to delete its throwaway files before `npm run check`, or ignore `scratch/` in ESLint, which is a config change. Settled 2026-10-22 in chat: ESLint ignores `scratch/`. Joe approved the config change, and it's made in its own small PR before #77 starts.

- ~~On #109, after the cap, Joe also took `Bash(npx tsx:*)` off the reviewer's allowed tools, since `npx tsx` fails in the sandbox. The fix job's `--allowedTools` list starts from the replays' list, which has it too (see "Do").~~ Settled 2026-10-22 in chat: the fix job's `--allowedTools` leaves `Bash(npx tsx:*)` out, as code review design 4.5 says (PR #111).

- ~~A "Fixed" marker tells every later review to check the fix again, with no end. Example: round 1 posts finding A, and the fixer replies "Fixed". Round 2 posts finding B, that A's fix didn't work, and B gets "Not fixed: wrong". In round 3, the list from `review-input.ts` still tells the reviewer to check A's fix and post it again if the problem is still there, and to leave B alone. So the reviewer could post the same problem a third time. Deferred 2026-10-22 from #109's sixth review ([finding](https://github.com/nimbusscale/road-trip-agent/pull/109#discussion_r4352696590)). Joe left it unfixed, since it needs a disputed fix and then a "wrong" on the dispute.~~ One way, if it shows up in the loop: a line in the `review-pr` skill's step 6 saying that when two earlier findings make the same point, the later one's instruction wins. Accepted 2026-10-22 in chat: nothing is built for it now. If the loop shows it happening, add that line to the `review-pr` skill's step 6.

Agreed in chat on 2026-10-21, and moved to #93 on 2026-10-22. #76's replays ran one round per draft, so #93's rounds are the first test of the fixer reading earlier rounds' replies on one PR. 236.title: Look back at earlier option sets, and reopen a card after a pick

blocks.text: An option card shows only the newest set of options for a stop or a stay's lodging. Once the user asks for more options, or for a higher or lower tier, the earlier set is gone from the page. And once the user picks an option, the card closes for good. To look at the options again, the user has to ask the agent.

In Joe's Bar Harbor session on the live site on 2026-10-30 (agent session `89f4dea6-6cb9-4320-a917-c063620acca9`), he was on the fence between Twelve and Fore Street for the Portland dinner. He picked Twelve in turn 9. To compare the two again later, he would have had to ask the agent, since there was no way to bring the card back. Raised by Joe on 2026-10-30.
The data is already there, so this is a change to the API's view and the page, not to the trip:
- Every candidate is saved with a set number, and asking for more options adds a new set without removing the old ones (domain model 3.9).
- Selecting an option removes no candidates. Only turning one down does.
- The newest-set filter is in `optionCardOf()` in `src/api/itinerary-view.ts`. A stop or stay with a selection gets `card: null`.

The agent needs no change. Selecting from an older set, or from a reopened card, sends the same message as today, such as "Select Twelve for dinner in Portland." The agent already handles switching a pick by name in chat (functional spec 7.5).
A turned-down place is removed, so it won't show when looking back. That's fine, since the user said no to it.

- [Functional spec](https://github.com/nimbusscale/road-trip-agent/blob/main/design/functional-spec.md), section 7.5 (option cards). Its rules change: the card no longer closes for good once an option is selected, and the user can step back through earlier sets.
- [Domain model](https://github.com/nimbusscale/road-trip-agent/blob/main/design/domain-model.md), section 3.9 (candidates and set numbers).

- ~~What does the card show for a stop or stay with a selection? Proposal: no card by default, as today, plus a "See options" button that opens it. The open card marks the pick, and its newest set shows first.~~ Settled 2026-10-30, in chat:
  - The card still closes when the user picks, as today. A stop or stay with a pick shows the pick, plus a "See options" button.
  - The button opens the card in place, with the newest set first and the pick marked in it. Another button closes it again.
  - Selecting another option from a reopened card sends the same message as any card's Select, such as "Select Fore Street for dinner in Portland." The agent handles the switch, as it does when the user asks in chat.
  - The button shows only when the stop or stay has a candidate other than the pick. One whose only candidate is the pick, such as a place the user named, gets none.
  - As with every card, it shows only in a session's itinerary view, not on the trip page.

- ~~How does the user move between sets? Proposal: back and forward arrows on the card, with "Set 2 of 3" or similar. The newest set shows first.~~ Settled 2026-10-30, in chat:
  - Back and forward arrows on the card, with "Set 2 of 3" between them. The newest set shows first. The arrows show only when there's more than one set.
  - The count goes by position, not by the saved set number. A set whose candidates were all turned down is gone, so set numbers can skip.
  - "More options", "Higher tier", and "Lower tier" show only on the newest set. An older set shows only Select on each option. Their messages say "these", such as "Show me something nicer than these for dinner in Portland", and the agent reads "these" as the newest set.
  - When a new set arrives, the card goes back to the newest set.

- Do "More options", "Higher tier", and "Lower tier" stay on a reopened card for a selected item? Today, new options for a selected item get no card, and the agent names them in chat (functional spec 7.5). Proposal: keep the actions, and drop that rule, so the new set shows on the reopened card like any other.

- Should this come before "Redo the web UI with Claude Design" (#204)? Proposal: yes. That issue changes only how the app looks, and this changes what the page does. Built first, the redo then designs the arrows and the button along with the rest.

156.title: Coordinator prompt and tool description fixes

blocks.text: The coordinator's instructions and tool descriptions grew one issue at a time. Read together, in the coordinator's view file (`src/agent/coordinator.view.md`), they have gaps that make the agent's job harder than it needs to be, whatever model runs it. This issue collects those gaps, from Joe's review of the view file and an independent review of it, so they're fixed in one PR.

The bar for an item: a fix that's clearly good practice goes in here, with no evaluation needed first. That covers things a person using the same tools would need too, such as knowing what the app's terms mean. An item whose benefit is in doubt, such as one that adds tokens to every turn for a gain no one is sure of, isn't fixed here. It becomes a candidate for an agent evaluation instead.
- [Functional spec](https://github.com/nimbusscale/road-trip-agent/blob/main/design/functional-spec.md), section 4: the app's terms.
- [Technical spec](https://github.com/nimbusscale/road-trip-agent/blob/main/design/technical-spec.md), section 5.2: what the coordinator's instructions cover.
- [Tool design](https://github.com/nimbusscale/road-trip-agent/blob/main/design/tools.md): the tool descriptions.

1. **The app's terms aren't defined for the coordinator.** The instructions define anchors and stretches (technical spec 4.1), but not the terms from functional spec 4 that the tools are built on: stay, night, day, last day, leg, stop, and candidate. The model pieces them together from tool descriptions. Example: `add_stay` says "Adds a stay, with one day for each of its nights", and a rule says "Only a day that starts and ends at the same stay can be a rest day". The riskiest gap is how nights and days add up. A 3-night stay covers three days, and the last day has no night, so a 7-day trip has 6 nights of stays. Nothing tells the model this. It could add 7 nights for a 7-day trip and get 8 days. The trip length check would catch it, but the model would be fixing a mistake it didn't need to make.

The lines an itinerary read returns aren't explained either. Tool design section 4 says what an item means goes in the agent's instructions, and a read's lines are explained by the instructions. The trip brief follows this: the instructions explain each item, so `read_trip_brief` stays short. Nothing does the same for the itinerary. In a read of a day, nothing explains "in set 1", "Along the leg" or "Near the Springdale stay", "detour 38 m when offered", "with the drive buffer", "free time", or "Set time: 6:30 p.m." The `read_itinerary` description itself is fine. It says what each scope returns, which is specific to that tool.

A few more terms need a line. "Set" as a noun ("2 in set 1") is one batch of candidates, and the option card shows only the newest set (functional spec 7.5). Without that, the coordinator may recommend a set 1 candidate the user can't see on the card. "Search area" is where a stop's places are looked for. "Last day" means the trip's final day in the check results rule, but the rule on removing a night says "Removing a night always removes the stay's last day," meaning the last of that stay's days. Say that one another way. Drive time is named three ways: "drive time" in the planning rounds, "road time" in `set_waypoints` and the reads, and "driving with the drive buffer" in the reads. Say what each is, so the model compares the right one with comfortableDrivingInHours.

One repeat goes the other way. The bullets under "Reading the trip brief, the itinerary, and memory" say a whole read leaves out the rationale and the weather text, which the `read_itinerary` description already says. Tool design section 4 says the system prompt never repeats a tool's description.

Fix: add a section on the itinerary to the instructions, like the one on the trip brief. It defines the terms, drawn from functional spec 4, and says what each line of a read means. Drop the repeat from the reading bullets, and keep the rules there on when to read a stop or stay. Add the section to the list in technical spec 5.2.

Then review every tool description against the new section, so each term is defined in one place and used the same way everywhere. `compute_route` needs it most. Its description says "A stop is where the party stops, such as a town that might become a stay," and its points take a kind of "stop" or "passThrough". In the itinerary, a stop is a meal or attraction on a day, not a town. It also says "pass-through point" where `set_waypoints` says "waypoint" for the same idea.

2. **The rule for places the user names says to always call `find_in_trip` first, with no reason given.** `find_in_trip` exists because a whole read names only the selected places. It only counts the other candidates, so the coordinator doesn't know their names. The rule leaves that out, and it's broader than technical spec 7.1, which says to look up only "a name it can't find in context." As written, it sends the coordinator to `find_in_trip` for a place it already has an ID for, such as a selected restaurant from the whole read, and for a place that's clearly new to the trip. It also says to ask the user when no match is clearly the place, which fits a typo such as "Desert Rose", but not a place that isn't in the trip. `find_in_trip` always returns the 5 closest places, so when the user says "let's add Arches" on a trip with no Arches, none is close, and the rule has the coordinator ask "Did you mean Desert View Watchtower?" Fix: give the reason, and split the rule into three cases. For a place the coordinator already has an ID for, use it. For a place it doesn't have, that may be one the trip offered, use `find_in_trip`. Ask the user when a match is close but may not be the place. When none is close, the place isn't in the trip, so use `find_place`. For a place that's new to the trip, use `find_place`. Skipping `find_in_trip` for a new place is safe, since `select_user_place` refuses a place that's already a candidate on that stop, and its reply names any other stop or stay where the place is a candidate. Proposed wording, to replace the first bullet under "Places the user names" and change the second:

> A whole read names only the selected places. It only counts the other candidates, so you won't know their names unless a scoped read or a worker's reply showed them.
   > - When the user names a place you already have an ID for, use it.
   > - When they name one you don't have, and it may be a place the trip offered, look for it with find_in_trip. When a match is close but you aren't sure it's the place, ask the user, such as "Did you mean the Desert Pearl Inn, the hotel in Springdale?" for "Desert Rose". A shorter form of a name, such as "the Desert Pearl" for the Desert Pearl Inn, is clear, so don't ask. When none is close, the place isn't in the trip, so look it up with find_place.
   > - For a place that's new to the trip, such as one a friend recommended, use find_place.
Change technical spec 5.2 ("When the user names a place") and tool design 2.1 ("`find_in_trip` finds a place the user names") to match.

3. **The rule on when to raise warnings is unclear.** It says "Raise warnings at the end of the turn, for those still open, once no change is still being discussed with the user." "At the end of the turn" sounds like every turn, and "a change" is vague. It could be read as holding warnings until the whole trip is planned. It means holding them until the change the coordinator and the user are working on is settled, which can take several turns. The weather worker rule in technical spec 5.2 uses the same phrase and has an example. The coordinator's line has none. Fix: replace the line with this wording, and change technical spec 5.2 ("How to handle broken feasibility rules") to match:

> Raise warnings once a change is settled, not while you and the user are still working it out. A change can take several turns, such as adding a night and then going through the stops it moved. Raise them at the end of the turn where the user confirms the change or backs out of it, and only those still open. Example: adding a Big Sur night makes a 3-day trip 4 days. Don't raise the trip length while you're still going through the stops the night moved. If the user then removes the night, the warning is gone, and there's nothing to raise.

4. **`add_stay`'s description says where the stay goes in a way that only makes sense next to the input schema.** It says "Adds a stay, with one day for each of its nights, after the stay given or first." "The stay given" and "first" point to the `after` input without naming it, and "first" isn't quoted, though the input's description quotes it. The next sentence uses "first" again, with another meaning: "Needs the itinerary's start place, end place, and start date first." Fix: name the input, and say what "first" does. A starting point:

> Adds a stay, with one day for each of its nights. Give after the ID of the stay it follows, or "first" to put it before every other stay. The place is usually a town. The itinerary's start place, end place, and start date must be set before a stay can be added.

Check `update_stay`'s "where it goes" the same way. `add_stops` and `move_stop` aren't built yet, but take an `after` input too (tool design 2.1, "Where an item goes"). Add a line to tool design 2.1 that a description names the `after` input and says what "first" does, so they follow the same pattern.

5. **`update_day`'s start time takes "none" to mean the trip brief's usual start time.** "None" reads as "no start time," which isn't what it does. The day still starts at the usual start time. Fix: take "default" instead, for a day's start time only. A stop's set time keeps "none" (tool design 2.1, "Times are clock times"), since a stop with no set time really has none. Today only the start time uses `NO_TIME` in `src/tools/skeleton-input.schema.ts`, since the stop tools aren't built yet. Rename it for "default", and change tool design 2.1 to match.

6. **`find_place`'s description says "When you aren't sure where the place is, give its state."** The sentence is about the `where` input, but doesn't name it. It means: when you don't know the town, give the state rather than guess a town. It reads as if the state were optional. And `where` takes "a town, region, or state," so a region with no state, such as "Big Sur", is allowed, though it's the case where the state helps most. The app plans only US trips, so every place has a state. Fix: drop the sentence from the description, and say it in `where`'s input description instead. A starting point:
> A town or region with its state, or only the state when you aren't sure where the place is, such as "Moab, UT", "Big Sur, CA", or "Utah".
Change the `find_place` row in tool design 2.3 to match.

7. **The instructions describe a write's check results differently from what the tools return.** "Tools that change the trip" says each write "replies with the feasibility check results the change made new, changed, or gone, anywhere in the trip." The reply (`src/tools/check-results-reply.ts`) also lists the already-known results for what the write touched, and marks a warning the user approved as "approved", such as "New warning, approved: …". The instructions never say what "approved" means, what "open" means in "warnings that are still open", or that a warning must be raised while a note is the coordinator's call (technical spec 8). Example: after a write, the coordinator sees "New warning, approved: Day 4 drives 7 h", and raises a warning the user already accepted. Fix: say what the reply lists, as technical spec 8 does ("What comes back"). Say each result is a warning or a note: a warning must be raised, and whether to mention a note is up to the coordinator. Say a warning marked approved is one the user accepted, so it isn't open, and isn't raised again.

8. **The memory section contradicts itself.** It says user memory holds standing preferences "such as their usual driving hours, route preference, budget, meal habits". Then "Writing memory" says "Don't save what the trip brief or the itinerary holds", and the trip brief holds those items for this trip. Example: the user says "we never drive more than 5 hours, on any trip." The coordinator sets comfortableDrivingInHours and skips user memory, so the next trip doesn't know. The rule is meant for trip memory. Fix: make it "Don't save to trip memory what the trip brief or the itinerary holds". The rule is only in `src/agent/coordinator-prompt.ts`, so add it to the "Writing memory" bullets in technical spec 5.2 too.

9. **Nothing tells the coordinator to keep IDs out of chat.** Technical spec 7.1 says "Users never see IDs." Every read and write reply is full of them, such as `stop_k7m2x9qa`, and the only rule about IDs in the instructions is for memory items. Example: "I moved breakfast (stop_k7m2x9qa) to Day 3." Fix: add to Conduct, such as "Never show IDs to the user. Name places, days, and stops in words." Add it to the conduct bullet in technical spec 5.2.

10. **"Where the road is still open" reads as a road closure.** The skeleton bullet says "set waypoints on scenic legs where the road is still open". It means the part of a leg that no stop the user chose already decides (technical spec 4.2: "The route preference is for the stretches nobody has decided"). "Open" also means an unsettled warning elsewhere in the instructions. Example: the coordinator checks for seasonal closures, and sets scenic waypoints on a leg whose road the user's own stops already chose. Fix: say "where no stop the user chose already decides the road", and change technical spec 4.2 to match.

11. **`find_place` says "Every match is saved to the trip."** Item 2 uses "in the trip" to mean in the itinerary, and `find_in_trip` searches only the itinerary. A place `find_place` saved isn't in it. Example: after a `find_place` lookup, the coordinator expects `find_in_trip` to find the place later, and it doesn't. Fix: "Every match is stored, so its place ID works in the other tools. That doesn't add it to the itinerary."

12. **`remove_stay` says it's "Refused while any stop is on its days, or any stop anywhere is near it."** "Near it" sounds like distance on a map. It means a stop on another day whose search area is this stay. Fix: say that.

13. **Some text is repeated between the instructions and the tool descriptions,** which tool design section 4 says never to do, since the copies can drift apart:
    - "Stays can't be added until all three are set" in the discovery round, and `add_stay`'s "Needs the itinerary's start place, end place, and start date first."
    - "Only a day that starts and ends at the same stay can be a rest day" in "Days and approvals", and the same in `update_day`.
    - "Removing a night always removes the stay's last day" in "Changes to stays", and `update_stay`'s "Changing the nights adds or removes days at the end of the stay's days."
    - The `tierRule` input's "The rule that produced the tier", which says what the item means. By tool design section 4 that belongs only in the instructions, which already say it in the skeleton bullet on tiers. The input gives only the format.

Fix: keep each fact in one place. Where a rule in the instructions depends on one, such as the advice on losing a different day when a night is removed, it can rely on the description instead of repeating it.

14. **The rule for a refused trip brief update conflicts with the limit rules.** It says "If the error gives a limit, such as the maximum daily driving, send the whole update again with that item at the limit, and tell the user it's set to the maximum." The rules on trip length and comfortable driving hours say to push back instead: propose a trip that fits, or recommend fewer hours and ask what's comfortable. The refusal only happens once the coordinator has already ignored the limit in its instructions and in the input's description, and the error gives the limit too. So a fourth place that says what to do adds nothing, and the coordinator can judge what to do next. Fix: drop that sentence. Keep "nothing in it was saved", which tells the coordinator to send the other items again. That's specific to this tool, so move it into `update_trip_brief`'s description, and drop the bullet from the instructions. Change technical spec 5.2 and the `setComfortableDriving()` refusal in domain model 4.2, which says "so the coordinator can send it again at the limit", to match.

15. **The coordinator can't see whether "the route already goes through" an area.** The skeleton bullet on must-see areas says to add a waypoint "unless the route already goes through." No tool returns a route's path, only times and distances. Fix: say it's a judgment from the coordinator's own knowledge of the roads, such as UT-24 running through Capitol Reef, and to add the waypoint when it isn't sure.

16. **Nothing says what to do when the user asks to forget a trip brief item.** The instructions say "Trip brief items can be changed, but not forgotten," and that when the user asks to forget an item, forget it, which is about memory. Fix, as a starting point:

> When the user asks to forget a trip brief item, explain that it can be changed but not forgotten. For restDaysText or budgetRulesText, change its text to say there's none, such as "no budget rules."
Only these two optional text items can say there's none. A required item can't, as item 17 says.

17. **Nothing says what "required" means for a trip brief item.** The instructions say each item is required except three, and to establish each one. They don't say what to do when the user says "we don't really have any interests" or "no must-sees". A model could save "none" and move on. The app plans trips to see and do things, not only routes between hotels, so "none" isn't an answer for a required item. Fix, as a starting point:
> Required means a real answer. When the user has none, help them find one, such as by suggesting what the focus is known for. Don't save "none".

18. **"Confirm it and push back" can read as accept it.** The rule on comfortable driving hours says "When the user gives more than 6, confirm it and push back." "Confirm" can mean accept and save it. It means check that they mean it. Fix: "check that they mean it, and push back". Change functional spec 5.2 and technical spec 5.2, which say "confirms it and pushes back", to match.
More items are added here as the review goes on.

- Make each item's fix in the coordinator's instructions (`src/agent/coordinator-prompt.ts`), the tool descriptions, and the design doc each one belongs in.
- Run `npm run agent-views`, and commit the coordinator's view file with the change.
- The coordinator's view file shows each item's fix.
- The design docs match the instructions and tool descriptions.
- `npm run check` passes.
A PR.

209.title: Saving to the right place: trip brief, itinerary, or trip memory, checked with an evaluation

blocks.text: What the user says can be saved in three places: the trip brief, the itinerary, or trip memory. Each has its own job. The trip brief is what the user wants from the whole trip (functional spec 5.2). The itinerary holds the plan: the places, the dates, and the stays (functional spec 4). Trip memory holds what doesn't fit either, such as a soft intention ("wants one nice dinner in Austin"), why the user chose something, or an open item (functional spec 10.2). No fact is kept in two places (functional spec 5.2).

The coordinator sometimes saves something in the wrong place. That matters because each place is used differently later. Must-sees are anchors: the coordinator builds the route around them, selects a one-place must-see right away in the fill, and the "must-sees vs days" check treats each one as required (technical spec 4.1 and 5.2). So a "maybe" saved as a must-see can later be planned as if it were fixed. A fact saved in both the itinerary and trip memory goes stale in memory when the plan changes.

A wish, such as "maybe whale watching" or "definitely like to see Portland", goes in trip memory (the Bar Harbor turn 2 case). The trip brief's text items are each described as "In the user's words" (`src/tools/trip-brief-input.schema.ts`), which pushes the coordinator to copy what the user said whole. Let it sort the user's words into the item each part belongs in, so a "maybe" stays out of the must-sees and goes in the interests or trip memory instead. Decided by Joe on 2026-11-10, in chat, from the labeling (set 2: "maybe the Hemingway house" in both the interests and the must-sees).

Run the evaluation again. The implementer drafts the wording, and Joe reviews it in the PR. Run `npm run agent-views`, and commit the coordinator's view file with the change. Record the results before and after in the PR.

- **Single turns first, multi-turn tests only if needed.** Decided by Joe on 2026-11-09, in chat. Start with the single-turn replays above. A replay of a later turn starts from the trip as the old code saved it, so after a fix it can test a trip the new code would never have built. Example: if the fix makes Natick turn 1 save the Berkshires to trip memory, a replay of turn 5 still starts with them in the must-sees. If the results show that matters, add multi-turn tests that start from an empty trip, play the opening of a trip, and check what was saved after each step. [LangWatch Scenario](https://langwatch.ai/scenario/) is one way to run them. Its script can mix fixed user messages with turns a simulated user writes (`scenario.proceed`), and code checks can run between steps, reading the trip brief, the itinerary, and trip memory from the database. It would run inside a Phoenix experiment, with `run-turn`'s setup as a fixture and the judges as Phoenix evaluators. Nothing here needs settling before work starts.
- The results are recorded, with how many runs passed. If the guidance changed, the results before and after are both recorded.
- The golden set is in Phoenix, with the judge's false alarms and misses against it recorded in this issue.
- The evaluation stays in the set, so later changes rerun it.
- `npm run check` passes.
More than one PR. #287 holds the reading pages for step 1 of the labeling. The rubric, the judge, and the replays come in later PRs (Joe, 2026-11-10, in chat).

**Evaluate** when #132 is done.

When this is done, the agent's behavior can be checked again after any change to its instructions, its tools, or its model, by running a set of evaluations. Without them, the only way to tell whether a change made the agent better or worse is Joe testing by hand.
- [DEVELOPMENT.md](https://github.com/nimbusscale/road-trip-agent/blob/main/DEVELOPMENT.md), section 5.
- [Technical spec](https://github.com/nimbusscale/road-trip-agent/blob/main/design/technical-spec.md), section 3.1 (tests).
- [Functional spec](https://github.com/nimbusscale/road-trip-agent/blob/main/design/functional-spec.md), section 11.

- Which framework runs the evaluations? promptfoo is the likely choice. Check its current docs, and that it can run the app's coordinator through the Agent SDK on the Claude Max plan (systems design, section 5).
- How is each result scored: by what was saved, such as the trip brief and memory, by a model reading the reply, or both?
- How much of the Claude Max plan does one run of the evaluations use?
- How do the simulated user (#66) and the acceptance tests (#69) fit with the evaluations?

- ~~Do #66, #67, #68, and #69 still make sense as written? They're the testing and checking work after the workers, and they were planned before the evaluations in Phoenix and the evaluation issues, such as #167, #177, and #185. Look at them again together with this issue and those. Raised by Joe on 2026-10-28.~~ Settled 2026-11-04 in chat: #66 becomes the setup for a simulated user on any harness and model, such as Codex with a GPT model. It chats through `npm run live-chat` (#251), a terminal client for the app's API, signed in as its own Supabase user, and is shaken out with a whole San Francisco trip on the local stack. #67 and #68 become the first trips recorded on the live site for the corpus. They check how the simulated user behaved and what was saved to the trip brief, not that the itinerary matches domain model section 5, since live places and the workers' picks change from run to run. #69 stays as written. Traces in the `road-trip-agent-local` Phoenix project are throwaway, and the `road-trip-agent` project holds the sessions to evaluate.

- Which evaluations watch for these `update_trip_brief` mistakes? Tool descriptions start lean, with no example of a whole call. One is added only when an evaluation shows a mistake it would fix. The mistakes:
  - Sending every item on every call, when only one changed.
  - Splitting one change into a call per item.
  - Summarizing the user in a text item, such as `mustSeesText`, instead of using their words.

- Should an evaluation cover how an agent judges a place's budget tier, value, mid-range, or posh, at the edges between tiers? A place could fit two tiers, depending on how it's looked at. Nothing defines where one tier ends and the next starts yet (#60). Raised while going through the coordinator's view file, `src/agent/coordinator.view.md`.

- ~~Should an evaluation check that the coordinator keeps itinerary facts out of trip memory? No fact is kept in both (functional spec 5.2). In Joe's terminal run on 2026-10-23, the coordinator saved "Trip starts and ends in Austin. The user flies out of Austin the night of Sunday, February 14, 2027" to trip memory. The start and end places and the dates belong in the itinerary. The flight that evening belongs in memory, since the itinerary can't hold it. #55 changes the coordinator's memory instructions to say so. It also adds `update_itinerary`, so the evaluation can't run before #55 is merged. Raised by Joe on 2026-10-23, while settling #55's open questions.~~ Moved to #209 on 2026-10-28.

- May the coordinator add a note for itself to a memory item, beyond the user's words? In all five runs of the #132 spike, it did. "We never eat at chains" became "Never eats at chain restaurants. Suggest only independent, local places for meals." "Skip I-35 this time" became "Avoid I-35 on this trip. Plan routes out of Austin that don't use it, and set waypoints if a leg would default onto it." The judge's rubric didn't say whether that counts as a rule the user didn't state, so it graded the same wording both ways ([research/agent-evaluations.md](https://github.com/nimbusscale/road-trip-agent/blob/main/research/agent-evaluations.md), section 2.5). Raised by the #132 spike on 2026-10-24.

- Should functional spec 10.2's example change? It gives "no chain restaurants" as trip memory, but the #48 check expects "we never eat at chains" in user memory. The "never" is what makes it a standing preference. Raised by the #132 spike on 2026-10-24.

- ~~How do the user's message and the right token counts get into each turn's trace? The Agent SDK instrumentation shows the streamed prompt as `{}`, and leaves cache tokens out of its input count, so a 48,255-token turn shows as 8. The spike branch fixes both with spans from our own code in place of the instrumentation: one for the turn, and one for each model call and each tool call, with each call's thinking and tokens. Workers aren't covered yet ([research/agent-evaluations.md](https://github.com/nimbusscale/road-trip-agent/blob/main/research/agent-evaluations.md), sections 2.2 and 3). Raised by the #132 spike on 2026-10-24.~~ Moved to #135 on 2026-10-25.

- ~~How is `@arizeai/phoenix-client` installed for good? It names `@anthropic-ai/sdk` `^0.35.0` as an optional peer, and the app has 0.135.0, so `npm install` fails without `--legacy-peer-deps`. The spike tested an `overrides` entry in `package.json` that fixes it with no flag ([research/agent-evaluations.md](https://github.com/nimbusscale/road-trip-agent/blob/main/research/agent-evaluations.md), section 3). Raised by the #132 spike on 2026-10-24.~~ Moved to #282 on 2026-11-05.

- Where do experiments send their traces and results? The #132 spike ran Phoenix on Joe's machine, under the `evals` Compose profile. #135 runs one Phoenix on the server, reached from Joe's machine through an SSH tunnel, with the server's traces in the `road-trip-agent` project and local ones in `road-trip-agent-local`. So the experiments could use that Phoenix too, through the tunnel, or a local Phoenix of their own. Raised on 2026-10-25, while writing #135.

- Which evaluations check how the coordinator finds a place the user names? #152 adds `find_in_trip`, which searches the trip's own places, next to `find_place`, which searches Google. So there are two tools for a place the user names. The coordinator should call `find_in_trip` first, and `find_place` only for a place that isn't in the trip (technical spec 5.2). `find_in_trip` always returns the 5 closest places, so the coordinator also has to notice when none is the place meant. Example: the user wants a new restaurant, Desert Rose Grill, and the closest match is the Desert Pearl Inn. It should ask, not select the inn. And when `select_user_place` says the place is also a candidate on another stop (#56), it should notice, and fix the pick or ask. Raised on 2026-10-26, from #129 ([research/itinerary-read-size.md](https://github.com/nimbusscale/road-trip-agent/blob/main/research/itinerary-read-size.md), sections 6.3 and 6.4).

- Should the agents' prompts go in Phoenix's prompt registry? It keeps versions of a prompt, and its playground and experiments can run one against saved spans. It doesn't link a prompt to traces by itself: the app would set `llm.prompt_template.version` on the spans. #194 puts the app's commit SHA on each turn's span, and the view files at that commit show each agent's prompt and tools, so a registry version isn't needed just to see what an agent read. Our prompts are built in code, so the registry would hold a second copy. Raised on 2026-10-28, while settling #194. The judge prompts fit better. A rubric is one model call with a few slots, which is what Phoenix's playground runs. So rubric versions could be tried there against the judge's dataset, turns labeled by Joe, and compared turn by turn. Raised on 2026-11-03, in chat.

- Should a walkthrough of the prompts decide which behaviors get an evaluation? The design walkthroughs (reviews/walkthroughs/) had a fresh agent read only the design docs and play the user and every agent through the San Francisco and Moab trips, and they found many design gaps before any code existed. The same could be done with the agents' instructions and tool descriptions, as the view files show them: give an agent a view file and a trip, and have it say what it would call, and why. A problem that's clearly a wording mistake gets fixed, since a clear fix goes in without an evaluation. One where it's unclear whether a change helps becomes an evaluation candidate. Running it with a smaller model, such as Sonnet, may show where the wording leans on Opus to fill gaps. Caveat: a model saying what it would do isn't the same as what it does deep in a real conversation, so this finds wording problems, not behavior. Running the real coordinator with faked tool replies and a model playing the user would show behavior.

- When should real traces be scored after the fact? Phoenix can run evaluators over traces that already exist, and attach the scores to their spans, with nothing run again. Code would pick out the suspect cases, and a judge model would decide the fuzzy ones. Example: code finds each `find_place` call with no earlier `find_in_trip` call in the session. A judge then decides whether the place was one the user named, and whether an earlier search was for the same place, such as "Desert Rose" and "Desert Rose Grill". Some mistakes need only code, such as an `update_trip_brief` call that resends an item with the value it already had. A score over traces is a rate, such as 3 of 40 turns, not a pass or fail. There are few real traces today, so this waits until simulations or walkthroughs make more. Raised by Joe on 2026-11-03, in chat.

- How are the evaluations built up? This is a provisional plan, not a commitment. It's what we're working toward, and it can change as we go. Sketched by Joe and Claude in chat on 2026-11-03, after running Phoenix's built-in evaluators on the Bar Harbor session:
  - Joe learns more of Phoenix first, through its tutorials.
  - Record more sessions to build a corpus. Joe and his wife each plan a trip. Simulated users play the San Francisco and Moab trips on the live site (#66, #67, #68). Any harness and model can play one, such as Claude Code, a GPT model through Codex, or an open-weight model.
  - A simulated user gets a trip file, a persona file, and its instructions, with no hooks steering it (#66). The trip file holds the facts it knows (dates, places, budget, driving limits), things it hasn't decided, and changes partway through, such as skipping Denver once the first draft is done. The persona file says how it talks, such as curt or impatient. Its prompt says to answer only what's asked, give one or two facts at a time, and stick with any answer it makes up. The trip file also works as an answer key, to check what the agent saved to the trip brief.
  - Write one general evaluator first, to learn the process. It covers how the agent does on any turn, not one behavior. Phoenix's built-in rubrics don't fit a long planning conversation: on Bar Harbor, correctness marked 22 of 23 turns incorrect. So the rubric is our own, using the built-ins only as a starting point. Start with "grounded in the record": every place, hour, distance, or price in a reply comes from a tool result or the trip record. Two strong models, such as Opus and a GPT 6.1 model, label turns from the corpus, each on its own. Code compares their labels, and Joe looks only at the turns where they disagree. No turns are labeled by hand. Then compare the judge's labels to theirs, and refine the rubric until they agree. Decided by Joe on 2026-11-05, in chat. The corpus is the sessions with a `corpus` session annotation in the `road-trip-agent` Phoenix project: 21 sessions, 3 `real_user` and 18 `simulated_user`, labeled on 2026-11-05. The first general evaluator, "grounded in the record", moved to #282 on 2026-11-05, with what it checks, what the judge reads, and how the labeling runs. Two or three general evaluators may follow, such as these:
    - "Request handled": the reply does what the user asked.
    - "The reply is for the user": it tells the user what they need to know, and doesn't think out loud. On a new trip, one reply began "I need to read brief and memory first." That's a note the coordinator wrote to itself, before its tool calls, and the user saw it. #65 adds a line to the instructions against it. This evaluator shows whether it still happens. Raised by Joe on 2026-11-04, in chat.
    - "Fits the trip": what the reply says makes sense given the itinerary. In #282's sample, a Moab reply chose a hotel and said "after a day of hiking, you'll also have a pool and a hot breakfast there". Its Day 2 leaves the hotel at 5:30 a.m. and doesn't come back until 8:02 p.m., so the hot breakfast doesn't fit that day. Each fact had a source, so "grounded in the record" passes it. Raised by Joe on 2026-11-06, in chat, while reviewing #282's first set.
    - "Tool use": it picks the right tool, with the right inputs, and doesn't call tools it doesn't need. Phoenix's built-in evaluators for tool use didn't work well on Bar Harbor, so the rubric is our own. It also answers a question moved from #65 on 2026-11-04: are about two dozen tools too many for the coordinator? If it chooses badly, merge the add, update, and remove tools for each kind of item.
  - The judge sees what the agent saw: the coordinator's system prompt from the commit on the turn's span, and the earlier turns with their tool calls. On Bar Harbor, adding that context changed tool response handling from 21 of 23 turns incorrect to 10.
  - Then write the behavior evaluations: the issues labeled "Eval Canidate", plus the ones listed in this issue. They can start from recorded sessions with `npm run run-turn` (#245), before any simulation exists.
  - Then run more simulated sessions (#66) to grow the corpus. Run both kinds of evaluation on them. A general evaluator gives a rate over many turns, such as 3 of 40. A behavior evaluation passes or fails on a case built to trigger the behavior.

- Do the evaluations run as Phoenix experiments, written in TypeScript? A dataset row would name a recorded turn (session, turn, and message) and what's expected of it. The experiment's task runs that turn with `npm run run-turn`, and code checks and judges score the result. Phoenix keeps each experiment's results, so a run before a prompt change and a run after it can be compared case by case. Joe leans toward TypeScript for the real evaluations, since they'd reuse app code such as `run-turn`, even though his Phoenix tutorials are in Python. Raised by Joe on 2026-11-03, in chat.
- Set up the framework, and a command that runs the evaluations against the local stack (systems design, section 6), outside `npm run check`.

- Start an evaluation of one turn from a recorded session with `npm run run-turn` (#245). It gives the coordinator the recorded conversation and the trip as it stood, and runs the turn on today's code. Leave the copied transcript lines as they are. The API drops each of the coordinator's earlier thinking blocks once anything before it in the conversation changes. In #245, rewriting the first message's date line dropped all 17 of them in the Bar Harbor session's turn 5 (persistence design, section 8.9).

- Watch the runs for the coordinator reacting to the two lines Claude Code adds that the recorded turn didn't have: its date change line, and an environment line with the local working folder (persistence design, section 8.9). #245 accepted both. If the coordinator reacts to either, look at it again.
- Turn the checks in #48 into evaluations: discovery fills in the trip brief, user or trip memory, confirming the usual driving hours on a second trip, and pushing back on 14 hours of driving.
- Write how the evaluations run into DEVELOPMENT.md section 5, in place of "How they run is settled when the first one is written."
- One command runs every evaluation and prints each result.
- Each evaluation passes against the current coordinator. A change made on purpose to break one, such as taking the driving hours line out of the instructions, makes it fail.

151.title: Make the whole itinerary read smaller

blocks.text: **Starts** once #150 and #148 are merged. #150 writes the design. #148 changes the "Lodging tier:" line in `src/tools/day-lines.ts`, which this issue changes too.

The coordinator can't read the whole itinerary of a long trip. A whole `read_itinerary` of a busy 14-day trip is about 34,500 tokens. That's over Claude Code's limit of 25,000 tokens for a tool result, so the tool refuses it. The coordinator reads the whole trip at the start of each session, after a resume, and for "what's left to decide?" (technical spec 5.2). So on a trip longer than about a week, it gets an error in all three.

#129 settled on a whole read that gives less. It gives each picked place with its town, and counts the other candidates by set. It leaves out the rationale, the weather text, and the rule behind each tier, which the itinerary view shows the user. That brings the busy trip to about 15,300 tokens. Reads of a day, stay, or stop don't change.

- [Tool design](https://github.com/nimbusscale/road-trip-agent/blob/main/design/tools.md), section 2.1: the `read_itinerary` row, and the sections "A whole read gives less than a scoped read", "A read has a size limit of 25,000 tokens", "A trip too large to read whole can't be planned any further", and "A scoped read too large to return gets a different error".
- [Technical spec](https://github.com/nimbusscale/road-trip-agent/blob/main/design/technical-spec.md), section 5.2 ("What a whole read gives") and 7.2 ("Reading the itinerary").

- For a longer example of the format than tool design 2.1 gives, `research/itinerary-read-size/slim-read-proposed.txt` is a whole 14-day trip in it, with its last stay still undecided. It's a mockup, written by a script, so where it and tool design 2.1 differ, tool design 2.1 wins.
- None.

- Change the whole read, `wholeLines()` in `src/tools/itinerary-lines.ts`, to the format in tool design 2.1. The lines are built in `src/tools/day-lines.ts` and `src/tools/stop-lines.ts`, at a level of detail, `"short"` or `"full"`. Today the whole read and a day read both use `dayLines(…, "short")`. The day read doesn't change, so the whole read needs a third level of detail, not a change to `"short"`. `stayLines(…, "short")` is used only by the whole read.

- These details of the format aren't spelled out in tool design 2.1:
  - **The town** comes from the same rule the short line uses, `townOf()` in `src/domain/place.ts`, which is private today. Expose it, such as with a `town` getter. A place with no town, such as a trail whose address has none, shows only its name and ID.
  - **The folded stop line** gives, after the name and ID: the town, then the detour time, then the visit time, as in `Selected: Valley of Fire State Park (place_…), Overton, detour 38 m when offered, visit time 2 h.` The detour time is the selected place's candidate's `detourTimeInMinutes`, and is left out when it's null.
  - **A count line** names each set with at least one candidate to count, in set order, counted from 1 (`setNumber + 1`), such as `3 in set 1, 2 in set 2.` For "Other candidates:", the selected place isn't counted, and a set left with none is skipped. With nothing left to count, there's no line. Today's `- Candidates:` and `- Lodging candidates:` blocks become one count line each, in the same place: indented under a stop, and at the stay's level for lodging.
