282.title: General evaluator: grounded in the record

blocks.text: This is the first general evaluator, and its main job is to teach the process of building one in Phoenix: writing a rubric, building a golden set with two strong models, tuning the rubric until a small judge model agrees with the golden set, and then scoring a whole corpus. A **general evaluator** checks how the coordinator does on any turn, not one behavior. This one asks a single question of each turn: is every fact in the coordinator's reply **grounded**, meaning it came from a source the coordinator had? It gives one verdict per turn, `grounded`, `not_grounded`, or `no_facts`, and lists the facts that weren't grounded. `no_facts` is for a reply with no facts to check, such as one that only asks questions, so those turns can be counted apart from the ones whose facts all check out. Added by Joe on 2026-11-06, in chat.

It scores only turns already recorded in Phoenix. Nothing is run again, and it doesn't lead to a prompt change. Whatever rate it finds is the result. The behavior evaluations (the issues labeled "Eval Canidate") are where turns get rerun with `npm run run-turn`, before and after a change.
Moved out of [Agent evaluations](https://github.com/nimbusscale/road-trip-agent/issues/53), from the bullet "How are the evaluations built up?" in its open questions.
- [DEVELOPMENT.md](https://github.com/nimbusscale/road-trip-agent/blob/main/DEVELOPMENT.md), section 5.
- [Systems design](https://github.com/nimbusscale/road-trip-agent/blob/main/design/systems.md), section 10: the turns' traces in Phoenix.
- `src/agent/coordinator.view.md`: what the coordinator sees, including the two sentences the rubric copies (below).
- [research/agent-evaluations.md](https://github.com/nimbusscale/road-trip-agent/blob/main/research/agent-evaluations.md), sections 2.3 to 2.6: the #132 spike's judge on Haiku, and what it cost.
Terms used here:

- **The corpus:** the sessions in the `road-trip-agent` Phoenix project that have a session annotation named `corpus`, with identifier `corpus`. Its label is `real_user` or `simulated_user`, and its metadata names the trip, who played it, and the run's issue. On 2026-11-05 that's 21 sessions and 301 turns: 3 sessions Joe and his family played, and 18 from 9 simulated user runs. Sessions with a `not_for_evaluation` annotation are left out.
- **A turn:** one `coordinator.turn` span, with the spans under it in its trace.

- **Labelers:** two models that label sampled turns, each working alone, both on high effort: Sonnet 5.5 in Claude Code, and GPT's Sol 6.1 in Codex. Opus 5.5 labeled the calibration sets in Sonnet's place. Neither sees the other's labels. The session that writes the rubric isn't a labeler.
- **Golden set:** the sampled turns with a settled label. That's either the label both labelers agree on, or Joe's call where he made one.
- **The judge:** Haiku 5.5, run with the rubric over the golden set, and then over the whole corpus.

- ~~How is `@arizeai/phoenix-client` installed for good? It names `@anthropic-ai/sdk` `^0.35.0` as an optional peer, and the app has 0.135.0, so `npm install` failed without `--legacy-peer-deps` in the #132 spike. The spike tested an `overrides` entry in `package.json` that fixed it with no flag (research/agent-evaluations.md, section 3). Check whether the current version still has the conflict. Moved from #53.~~ Settled by Joe on 2026-11-05, in chat: with an `overrides` entry. Checked the same day: 7.18.1 still names `^0.35.0`, which for a 0.x version allows only 0.35.x. Added to Do.

- ~~Later, should the allowed cases come from one shared piece of text? The coordinator's instructions and the rubric would both render it, so the rubric always matches the instructions at a given commit. That would remove the hand-copied sentences above. Raised by Joe on 2026-11-05, in chat. Not needed for this corpus.~~ Settled by Joe on 2026-11-05, in chat: not for this project. The hand copy stays.

- ~~Should the rubric say a fair reading or summary of sourced facts is grounded? In the first set, on rubric `4343ba1`, Opus flagged a reply that listed a hotel's sourced 4.6-star rating, "the highest-rated of the three", under "Why it was offered", since the hotel's "Why" note doesn't name its rating. Joe called it too fine a point: a true reading of sourced facts. Sol didn't flag it. Held until the second set shows whether it comes up again. Raised by Joe on 2026-11-06, in chat.~~ Settled by Joe on 2026-11-06, in chat: no rubric change. It didn't come up in the second set, where both labelers took fair readings of sourced facts as grounded. Raise it again if it comes back.
**Decided by Joe on 2026-11-05, in chat:**

- **What counts as grounded.** A fact in a reply is grounded if it came from any of these:
  - a tool result, from this turn or an earlier turn in the session. This includes trip tool results, such as `read_itinerary`, since code works out much of what they say, such as schedule times, drive times with the buffer, and check results.
  - a worker's result, as the coordinator received it.
  - the user's own words.
  - the coordinator's own knowledge, but only where its instructions allow it, or as a general, guidebook-level description of a well-known place, such as "the Ferry Building is known for its food hall."

Specific facts that can be checked always need a tool result: hours, prices, distances, drive times, addresses, whether a business exists, and current closures. The judge checks where a fact came from, not whether it's true. A made-up opening time fails even if it happens to be right.

- **Where the instructions allow the coordinator's own knowledge.** The rubric copies these two sentences from the coordinator's instructions, in `src/agent/coordinator-prompt.ts`, rather than giving the judge the whole system prompt:
  - From the trip sketches step: "Sketches come from your own knowledge, not from research. … Seasonal closures and hazards also come from your own knowledge at this stage."
  - From the waypoints rule: "No tool shows the road a route takes, so judge that from your own knowledge of the roads, such as UT-24 running through Capitol Reef."

Trade-off: the rubric holds a copy. If the instructions change what the coordinator may say from its own knowledge, the judge keeps grading against the old rule until the rubric is updated by hand. Both sentences last changed on 2026-10-26, before the oldest corpus session (2026-10-30), so the copy holds for the whole corpus.

- **What the judge reads for a turn,** built by code from the turn's spans and the earlier turns in the same session:
  - each user message and reply in the session so far, including the date line.
  - each of the coordinator's tool results, labeled with the tool's name. For the 8 tools whose result doesn't say what it changed, the call's input too: `add_memory_item`, `update_memory_item`, `forget_memory_item`, `update_trip_brief`, `update_itinerary`, `update_day`, `update_stop`, and `update_stay`. Example: `add_memory_item` replies only "Added mem_x to this trip's memory.", so without the input the judge can't check "I've noted that you don't want to see the same thing twice." The input isn't a source for facts. It only shows what a successful change did. Decided by Joe on 2026-11-06, in chat, after the first set.
  - each worker shown only by its result, the `Agent` span's output. The worker's own searches are left out, since the coordinator never saw them.
  - the reply being judged.

Left out: the system prompt, the other tools' inputs, and the coordinator's thinking. A tool call's input is the coordinator's own writing, so it isn't a source, and those tools' results already say what they did. Earlier sessions on the same trip are left out too, since the coordinator doesn't see them.

- **Every tool result counts as a source,** including text the coordinator wrote into the trip that a tool repeats back, such as a stop's purpose. Trade-off: a fact the coordinator made up, saved into the trip, and then repeated would pass. On 2026-11-05, every write to the trip in the live project since 2026-10-30 was checked, about 1,700 calls. The coordinator's writes held settings, such as a day's start time, the user's own words, and purposes. None held a made-up hour, price, or distance. The hours and distances in stop notes came from the workers' searches. If this starts to happen, code can mark the coordinator's own text in the results from the calls' inputs, so the judge doesn't have to tell them apart.
- **Only the coordinator is checked.** If a worker made a fact up, the coordinator passes for repeating it. Checking workers would be a separate evaluator.

- **TypeScript,** in `src/`, so `npm run check` covers it. It uses `@arizeai/phoenix-client` to read spans, write annotations, and run the experiments. The judge calls Haiku through the Anthropic SDK the app already has, with structured output in the labelers' JSON, and code works out the label the same way. Changed by Joe on 2026-11-06, in chat, from `phoenix-evals`' classifier, which can only return a label. Haiku through Claude Code on the 60 golden turns, listing every fact, matched 51 labels and found 92 of the 103 facts both labelers flagged. Listing only the ungrounded facts also matched 51, but found 87, and got more of Joe's close calls wrong.

- **The judge's prompt is a Phoenix prompt,** `grounded-judge`. The repo's `evals/grounded/rubric.md` stays the source. A command pushes each committed version to Phoenix, tagged with its commit, along with the model, `claude-haiku-5-5`, and high effort. The experiment fetches the prompt from Phoenix, so each experiment links to the prompt version it used. The judge uses `JUDGE_API_KEY` from `.env`. Decided by Joe on 2026-11-06, in chat.

- **Install `@arizeai/phoenix-client` with an `overrides` entry in `package.json`,** so it uses the app's `@anthropic-ai/sdk`. Its optional peer range, `^0.35.0`, doesn't fit the app's 0.135.0, and `npm install` fails without it. The other fix, `--legacy-peer-deps`, would have to be passed on every install, including the server's builds, and turns off the peer check for every package. The #132 spike tested the `overrides` entry (research/agent-evaluations.md, section 3). `phoenix-client` doesn't use the Anthropic SDK for anything this evaluator calls.

- **The labels are span annotations** on each turn's `coordinator.turn` span, all named `grounded`. Phoenix keeps one annotation per name and identifier on a span, so each labeler gets its own identifier, and writing again under the same identifier replaces only that one:
  - `sonnet-5.5` and `gpt-sol-6.1`, annotator kind `LLM`, for the labelers. The calibration sets also have `opus-5.5`, and the labelers tried there: `gpt-terra-6.1`, plus the medium-effort runs, with `-medium` on the end.
  - `joe`, annotator kind `HUMAN`, for Joe's calls.
  - `haiku-5.5`, annotator kind `LLM`, for the judge's corpus run. Its annotations are named `grounded-haiku`, not `grounded`. Phoenix's project page sums up annotations by name only, not by identifier, so under `grounded` the judge's rate would be mixed with the labelers' labels and Joe's calls on the 60 sampled turns. Decided by Joe on 2026-11-08, in chat.

Each has the label `grounded`, `not_grounded`, or `no_facts`. `grounded` scores 1 and `not_grounded` scores 0. `no_facts` has no score, so Phoenix's average leaves those turns out, and the label still shows the turn was judged. Decided by Joe on 2026-11-06, in chat. Each also has the ungrounded facts as its explanation, and the rubric's version in its metadata, with every fact the annotator listed. The version is the commit that last changed `evals/grounded/rubric.md`, such as `{"rubric": "abdae9d"}`, so `git show` gives the exact text. The labeling command refuses to run while the rubric has uncommitted changes. Decided by Joe on 2026-11-06, in chat. The first set's v1 labels say `v1`.

- **The golden set is a Phoenix dataset,** `grounded-golden`. Each example holds a turn's judge input and span ID, and its settled label. For the 15 turns Joe called, it also holds his ungrounded facts. Its metadata holds the set, where the label came from, and both labelers' ungrounded facts. Sol's list isn't treated as the truth, since Joe's calls on the 5 label splits all went against it. When Joe changes a call, the golden set command updates only the changed turns, as a new version of the dataset. Replacing the dataset would delete the experiments run on it. Each experiment is scored against the labels at the time it ran, so comparing versions across a label change means scoring them again against the current labels.

- **Each rubric version is a Phoenix experiment.** The judge runs with that version over the golden set, and a code check marks whether its label matches the settled one. Phoenix keeps each experiment, so versions can be compared turn by turn. Each experiment judges every turn 3 times, since a run's score moves by about 2 turns from one run to the next. Decided by Joe on 2026-11-07, in chat. The experiment's description is the rubric commit's subject line, so that subject says what the version changed. Decided by Joe on 2026-11-08, in chat.
**The steps, in order:**

1. **Pick the sample.** Code picks about 60 turns from the corpus, about one in five, with at least one from every session, and the same turns for both labelers. The pick is repeatable, such as from a fixed seed, and it's done in sets of 5.
2. **Build each sampled turn's judge input** as its own file, ending with that turn's reply, so a labeler can't see anything that came later in the session.
3. **Draft rubric v1** from the decisions above. Joe reviews its wording.

4. **Label a set of 5.** Opus and Sol each label the set alone, and return JSON listing every fact in each turn's reply, with its source and whether it's grounded. Code works out the label from the list: no facts is `no_facts`, any ungrounded fact is `not_grounded`, and otherwise `grounded`. With only the ungrounded facts, there's no telling whether a labeler checked a fact and passed it, or never saw it. Decided by Joe on 2026-11-06, in chat, after the first set. Code checks the JSON and writes the annotations. Each labeler runs from a folder outside the repo, as the simulated users do (`simulated-users/README.md`, "Start a harness"), so it doesn't load the repo's `CLAUDE.md` or Joe's own. Run Sol on high effort, which Codex shows as `GPT-6.1-Sol high`. Codex starts it on a lower effort by default, and Joe has had better results on high. Decided by Joe on 2026-11-06, in chat. Opus and Sol labeled the calibration sets.

5. **Joe reviews the set.** A review page shows each turn's judge input in a form that's easy for a person to read, since the raw spans in Phoenix are hard to follow. The page shows only the judge input, not the labels. The agent gives both labelers' labels and flagged facts in chat. For the first sets, Joe reviews every turn, agreements included, and looks into each one in chat with the agent's help. He tells the agent his call in chat, and the agent saves it as the `joe` annotation with a command. The review page only reads. Decided by Joe on 2026-11-05, in chat, and changed on 2026-11-06 to leave the labels off the page.
6. **Refine the rubric,** and repeat steps 4 and 5 with a new set of 5, until Joe says the rubric is good. The hope is two sets.

7. **Label the rest of the 60** with Sonnet 5.5 and Sol 6.1, both on high effort. On the two calibration sets, Sonnet matched Joe as well as Opus did, for less, and a rerun gave the same labels. Decided by Joe on 2026-11-06, in chat; the comparison is in a comment. The agent tells Joe in chat which turns the labelers disagree on, and Joe reviews only those, the same way.
8. **Build the golden set,** and run the judge on it as an experiment, one for each rubric version. Tune the rubric until Joe says the judge agrees well enough.

9. **Run the judge over the whole corpus,** writing the `haiku-5.5` annotations, named `grounded-haiku`. Report the rate, such as 12 of 301 turns not grounded, with what the ungrounded facts were like, in a comment on this issue.
10. **Write how the evaluator runs** into DEVELOPMENT.md section 5.
- The `grounded` annotations from both labelers, and Joe's calls, are on the sampled turns.
- The golden set is a dataset in Phoenix, with an experiment for each rubric version tried.
- The judge's `haiku-5.5` annotations, named `grounded-haiku`, from the final rubric version, are on all corpus turns, and the rate is reported in a comment here.
- `npm run check` passes.
A PR, with the code, the rubric, and DEVELOPMENT.md section 5. The run's results go in a comment on this issue.
**Settled in:** chat. Propose each answer to Joe in chat first, and write it in once he agrees.

169.title: Check in at the stay before a later stop

blocks.text: **Starts** once #176 is merged.

A day reaches its stay only at the end, so the itinerary can't show the party checking in at the hotel before a later stop. Users plan days that way: check in, freshen up, then go out to an evening event or dinner. The coordinator can say so in chat, but the schedule and the route don't show it, so the times and the drive are wrong for the day as the user will live it.

Free time is time nothing is planned for, worked out from the gap before a set time. What the party does with time, such as checking in or walking around town, is a stop. So checking in becomes a stop at the stay. After #176, every wait comes after the drive, just before the stop with the set time. So the free time after a check-in shows before the next stop with a set time, and the coordinator works out with the user what to do with it (see Decided).

Live site, session `session_5hf47qpn` (the Natick to Bar Harbor trip). The user said: "We would want to ideally check into our hotel before going to COA." Day 1 is Natick to Bar Harbor, with lunch on the way and the College of the Atlantic alumni event set for 6:00 p.m. The coordinator told the user "That gives you time to check in and freshen up before the College of the Atlantic event at 6:00," but the schedule drives straight to the college, then 8 minutes to Bar Harbor at 9:08 p.m.
The day the user wants: leave at 10:00, lunch on the way, check in at the hotel, free time there, drive to the college for 6:00, then drive back to the hotel after.

Domain model 4.7 already notes the same gap for a late-night stop: "Moab Day 4 is routed Capitol Gorge → Panorama Point → Torrey hotel, though the party really checks in first and drives out again at night."
- **Check-in can happen at any time.** Hotels have check-in times, such as 3:00 or 4:00 p.m., but nothing checks them. Decided by Joe on 2026-10-27, to keep the change small.

- **The free time after a check-in follows #176's rule,** so it comes after the drive to the next stop with a set time. On Day 1 above, the day reads: the drive to the hotel, a 30-minute check-in, the 8-minute drive to the college, then about 2 hours of free time before the 6:00 event. The coordinator raises that time with the user, and suggests something that fits it and the way from the hotel to the college, such as a stop in Bar Harbor itself, coffee, or a walk around the campus. A suggestion the user agrees to becomes a stop. If the user would rather stay at the hotel until it's time to leave for the event, the coordinator gives the check-in a longer visit time, such as 2 hours to check in, freshen up, and rest, so the free time goes away. Decided by Joe on 2026-10-27.

- [Domain model](https://github.com/nimbusscale/road-trip-agent/blob/main/design/domain-model.md), section 3 (Stay: `sleepsAt`; Stop), 4.1 (how the schedule is worked out), 4.6 (`StopsService`), and 4.7 (how a leg is routed, and the Moab Day 4 note).

- [Technical spec](https://github.com/nimbusscale/road-trip-agent/blob/main/design/technical-spec.md), section 5.2 (laying out days), section 6 (the workers that fill stops), and section 8 (the checks).
- [Tool design](https://github.com/nimbusscale/road-trip-agent/blob/main/design/tools.md), section 2.1 (`add_stops` and the other stop tools).
- [Functional spec](https://github.com/nimbusscale/road-trip-agent/blob/main/design/functional-spec.md), section 9 (the itinerary view).

- ~~How is a check-in held? Proposal: a stop of a new kind, beside meal and attraction, so it takes part in the day's order, `move_stop`, set times, and the schedule like any other stop. Its place is the stay's `sleepsAt`: the lodging once one is selected, and the town until then. So selecting a hotel moves it, and it never has candidates.~~ Settled by Joe on 2026-10-27: a stop of a new kind, `checkIn`, beside meal and attraction. It has no search area, since no worker searches for it, and no candidates. Its place is worked out by the calendar, not stored: the `sleepsAt` of the stay the party sleeps at that night (`endStayOf()` for its day). So selecting a hotel moves it, and moving it to another day with `move_stop` takes it to that night's stay. It has a place from the moment it's added, so it counts as selected, and `add_stops` re-routes the leg when it adds one. Code that routes, schedules, checks, or shows a stop reads its place from the calendar, in place of `selectedPlace`. `add_stops` takes only its kind, purpose, and set time.

- ~~Which stay can it be at? Proposal: only the stay where the party sleeps that night, so never on the last day.~~ Settled by Joe on 2026-10-27: it follows from the answer above. The last day has no stay to sleep at, so adding or moving a check-in there is refused. A stay can't be removed while a stop is on its days, so a check-in's stay can't go away under it. A day holds at most one check-in, so adding or moving a second one onto a day is refused. Joe couldn't think of a day that needs two that's worth supporting.

- ~~How long is its visit? Proposal: the coordinator sets it, as for an attraction the user names, such as 30 minutes to check in and freshen up.~~ Settled by Joe on 2026-10-27: a new setting, the check-in visit time, of 30 minutes (technical spec section 10). Every check-in starts with it, the way a meal gets the meal visit time, so `add_stops` takes no visit time. The coordinator changes it with `update_stop` when the user wants longer, such as 2 hours to rest at the hotel until the event (see Decided).

- ~~What do the workers and checks do with it? Proposal: no worker fills it, and the opening hours check skips it.~~ Settled by Joe on 2026-10-27:
  - **Workers:** none fills it. A worker gets a stop only through its search area, and a check-in has none.
  - **Opening hours:** the three opening hours checks skip it. Google often has no hours for a hotel, so every check-in would get the "not known" note. Check-in times aren't checked (see Decided).
  - **Stop order:** a check-in splits the day into two parts for the check, like two short days. Google can't hold one stop in place while it reorders the rest, and it would nearly always move the check-in to the end, next to the hotel. On Day 1 that order saves about 16 minutes, over the 15-minute stop-order minimum saving, so every day like it would get a note to check in after the event. So the check-in stays where the coordinator put it. Google picks the best order of the stops before it, from where the day starts to the check-in's place, and of the stops after it, from there to where the day ends. Each part is ordered only when it has two or more selected stops, so Day 1 needs no call. `timeSavedInMinutes` is the two savings added, and `stopsInBestOrder` is the two parts joined, with the check-in in its place.
  - **The other checks** need nothing new. Daily driving counts the drives to and from the hotel, since the party drives them. Weather activities hold only attractions, and a check-in has no search area to not fit its day.

- ~~When does the coordinator add one? Proposal: when the user asks to check in before a later stop, or when the day has a stop near the stay after the party would have arrived, such as Moab Day 4's stargazing.~~ Settled by Joe on 2026-10-27: when the user asks to check in before a later stop, the coordinator adds one. When the day has a stop after the party reaches the stay's town, such as Moab Day 4's stargazing at 1 a.m., the coordinator suggests checking in first, and adds the check-in once the user agrees, as in #176. It doesn't add one as the day's last stop, since the day already ends at the stay. That's guidance in the coordinator's instructions, not a rule in code. After a check-in, the free time handling in Decided applies: on Moab Day 4, the coordinator raises the long evening before the stargazing, and suggests dinner or a longer check-in visit time.
- Write the answers to the open questions into the design docs.
- Build it in the domain, the tools, and the itinerary view, with tests using fakes (DEVELOPMENT.md section 5).

- Add the coordinator's rule for when to add one, and how it handles the free time after one (see Decided), in `src/agent/coordinator-prompt.ts` and technical spec 5.2. The implementer drafts the wording, and Joe reviews it in the PR. Run `npm run agent-views`, and commit the coordinator's view file with the change.
- A test shows a day like Day 1 above: the drive to the stay, the check-in, the drive to the event, free time before its set time, then the drive back to the stay.
- A test shows the same day with a longer check-in visit time: the party leaves the hotel just in time for the event, with no free time before it.
- Selecting a lodging for the stay moves the check-in to it, and re-routes the leg.
- A test shows the stop-order check splits a day at its check-in: the check-in keeps its place, and only the stops before it, or after it, are reordered.
- `npm run check` passes.
A PR.
**Settled in:** chat.

87.title: Check which files the reviewer reads on each PR

blocks.text: The reviewer, the `review-pr` skill in `.claude/skills/review-pr/`, is told in its step 4 to read `DEVELOPMENT.md` and `design/README.md` in full, and then only the design docs the PR touches. On #83, its last run read only the diffs of those two files, since the PR changed both. If it skips them on a PR that writes app code, it reviews without the coding rules. That would show up as missed findings, not as an error.

`design/code-review.md` was also split on #83: the rubric moved to `design/review-rubric.md`, so the reviewer reads the rubric without the real past reviews in `code-review.md`. That only works if the reviewer doesn't open `code-review.md` anyway. On a PR that doesn't touch the review code, it has no reason to.
- Code review design section 4.1, what the reviewer does.

129.title: Spike: whole itinerary reads of long trips

blocks.text: **Starts** once #54 is merged.

The coordinator can't read the whole itinerary of a long trip. #54 built `read_itinerary`, and measured a whole read of a 14-day trip at about 38,000 tokens. Claude Code returns at most 25,000 tokens of a tool result, so the tool refuses the read with an error. Technical spec 5.2 has the coordinator read the whole itinerary at the start of each session, after a resume, and to answer "what's left to decide?". On a trip longer than about a week, it gets the error in all three. This spike finds out how to handle that: read less in those cases, put less in a whole read, or allow a larger reply.
- [Tool design](https://github.com/nimbusscale/road-trip-agent/blob/main/design/tools.md), section 2.1 (`read_itinerary`, its size limit, and the measurement).

- [Technical spec](https://github.com/nimbusscale/road-trip-agent/blob/main/design/technical-spec.md), sections 5.2 (when the coordinator reads the whole itinerary) and 7.2 (what the coordinator sees).

**The trip measured.** A 14-day loop from Las Vegas with 8 stays, five stops a day, three candidates for each stop and stay, and a second set of three for about one in four of them. That's 312 candidates. It's `src/domain/fourteen-day-example.fake.ts`. Its places are made up, but each has the length of a real Google name, type, and address. Tool design 2.1 had estimated a trip like this at about 300 candidates and 20,000 tokens.

**The size of its whole read.** 72,264 characters, in 683 lines. The API counts it as 38,271 tokens for `claude-opus-5-5`, the coordinator's model. That's 1.89 characters a token. Plain English, the first 20,000 characters of DEVELOPMENT.md, came to 2.9. Tokens were counted by sending the text through the Agent SDK and taking the input tokens less those of a one-word prompt, since the plan token has no API key for the token count endpoint.
**Where the tokens go.** Measured on an earlier version of the read, at 75,613 characters:

- The 312 candidate lines were 44,832 characters and 23,183 tokens, about 60% of the read. Each gives its set, name, place ID, short line, and visit and detour times. The selected one also gives its rationale.
- Everything else was 30,800 characters and 16,177 tokens: stays, days, legs, schedules, stop lines, and check results.
- The read holds 496 IDs, such as `place_k7m2x9qa`. IDs and short lines are what make the read cost more tokens than prose.

**Scoped reads.** Each day of the trip reads at 5,202 characters at most. A stay read gives every candidate's full details, so a 3-night stay is 28,104 characters, and a 1-night stay about 12,000. A stay of 5 nights or more at this density would be refused too.

**What the tool does now.** It refuses any reply over 40,000 characters, about 21,000 tokens at 1.89, with "Can't read the itinerary: it's too large to return. Read one day, stay, or stop at a time instead." At this density, a whole read fits a trip of about a week.

**What Claude Code does over the limit.** It saves a tool result over 25,000 tokens to a file, and gives the model only the file's path and a short preview. The coordinator has no Read tool, so for it the result is cut off, with nothing to say so. 25,000 is Claude Code's default for MCP tools, and nothing in Claude Code 2.1.301, which SDK 0.3.301 ships, treats in-process servers differently.
**Every read stays in context.** A 38,000-token read at the start of each session uses that much of every later turn's input, and goes out of date with the next change.

[Research doc: making a whole itinerary read smaller](https://github.com/nimbusscale/road-trip-agent/blob/main/research/itinerary-read-size.md) (`research/itinerary-read-size.md`) measures a realistic 14-day read, what each change to the format would save, and what each costs the coordinator. Today's whole read of a busy trip is 66,260 characters and 34,498 tokens. The proposal in its section 5 brings it to 27,582 characters and 15,291 tokens. `research/itinerary-read-size/slim-read-proposed.txt` shows the proposed format, on the same trip with its last stay still undecided.

- ~~In each of the three cases in technical spec 5.2, what does the coordinator need from the read? Example: "what's left to decide?" needs empty and proposed stops and lodging, and open warnings, not every candidate.~~ Settled on 2026-10-26, in chat: the start of a session needs the open warnings, the forecast notes, and the trip as it stands. A resume needs the same, and also has to spot what the conversation never heard about (#147 asks whether to add a list of changes). "What's left to decide?" needs the empty and proposed items, the open warnings, and the approvals. None needs every candidate. Research doc section 2.1.

- ~~Can a whole read carry less, and still do its job? Example: each stop's selected place and a count of its other candidates, leaving the full list to a read of the stay or stop. Tool design 2.1 says a whole read gives every candidate, so this would change it.~~ Settled on 2026-10-26, in chat: yes. The whole read gives each picked place with its town, counts the other candidates by set, and leaves out the rationale, weather text, and tier rules, which the itinerary view shows. Research doc section 5.

- ~~Should there be a new scope for a summary, such as one for what's left to decide?~~ Settled on 2026-10-26, in chat: no. The slimmer whole read is about 15,000 tokens on a busy 14-day trip, and answers "what's left to decide?" itself.

- ~~Could the coordinator read a long trip a stay at a time in those cases, with only instructions changing?~~ Settled on 2026-10-26, in chat: no. It would lose the parts that only a whole read shows, and the slimmer whole read fits.

- ~~Should the limit go up? Claude Code has a setting for it, `MAX_MCP_OUTPUT_TOKENS`. Check whether it applies to an in-process server through the Agent SDK, and what a larger read costs in context on every later turn. Tool design 2.1 now says raising the limit isn't the fix, so a yes changes it.~~ Settled on 2026-10-26, in chat: no. The slimmer whole read fits under 25,000 tokens, and under the tool's 40,000-character limit, so neither changes. Research doc section 10.

- ~~Can the format itself cost fewer tokens, such as fewer IDs, without making a read harder for the coordinator to act on?~~ Settled on 2026-10-26, in chat: yes, in the ways research doc section 5 lists. Fewer IDs, no: the coordinator needs each one to act on its item (section 13).

- ~~Whichever way is chosen has to reach the parts that only a whole read shows today, raised in PR #128's review (finding comment-4364853766). The check results whose subject is the itinerary, such as the trip length ("The trip is 10 days, and the brief asks for 11."), are in no day, stay, or stop read, since each of those filters results by subject (`checkLines` in `src/tools/itinerary-lines.ts`). Nor are the start and end places, the dates, or the rejected places. So on a trip whose whole read is refused, the coordinator never sees them, and the start-of-session bullet on open warnings misses the trip length. A stay's lodging, lodging candidates, and weather text are only in a whole read or a read of that stay, never a day read (`dayScopeLines`). At the measured density, a stay of 5 nights or more is refused too, so for such a stay they can't be read at all. Reading a stay at a time leaves both cases open, and a slimmer whole read leaves the long stay open.~~ Settled on 2026-10-26, in chat: the slimmer whole read keeps the trip-level check results, the start and end places, the dates, the rejected places, and each stay's lodging line, so they stay in reach. A stay's weather text and lodging candidates come from a read of that stay. Research doc section 5.

- ~~If a whole read gives no candidate names (version L in the research doc), how does the coordinator find which stop or stay to read when the user names a candidate in chat, such as "let's do the Desert Pearl"? For lodging, `find_place` gives the town, which points to a stay. For a meal stop, a town can hold several stops, so it would read the whole stay or try stops one at a time. A wrong guess fails quietly: `select_user_place` refuses a place that's already a candidate only on that same stop, so on another stop it adds the place as one the user named, and the stop that offered it stays undecided. The options so far: keep each undecided item's candidate names, with or without place IDs, and measure both; or a `read_itinerary` scope by place ID. Research doc section 7 says the coordinator recovers after one wasted call, since the error tells it to use `select_candidate` (tool design 2.1, `select_user_place`). That's true only when it guessed the stop or stay that offered the place.~~ Settled on 2026-10-26, in chat: a new tool searches the trip's own places by name, with string similarity, and always returns the closest few with where each sits in the trip. The whole read gives counts, not names. Research doc section 6. Still open there: whether `select_user_place` should say when the place is a candidate on another stop or stay (section 6.4).
- ~~Measure what each option saves on the 14-day trip, in characters and in tokens as the API counts them.~~ Done in the research doc, in PR #140.
- ~~Propose an answer for each open question.~~ Done, and each is settled above.

- Now that PR #140 is merged, a new session writes the design changes in research doc section 11 into the design docs, in a PR. The research doc's sections 5, 6, and 9 hold the agreed details. The same session plans the build and opens its issues. It decides how to split the build, such as whether the read change and `find_in_trip` are one issue or two. Joe asked for that decision to be made there, not in the spike.
- Joe has agreed to an approach. Done on 2026-10-26: research doc sections 5, 6, and 9.
- The approach is written into the design docs: tool design 2.1, technical spec 5.1, 5.2, and 7.2, as research doc section 11 lists.
- The issues to build it are open.

An evaluation could check consistency instead of right answers: does a restaurant's tier agree with Google's price level where there is one, are a town's posh candidates never at a lower price level than its value ones, and does the same place get the same tier across runs? The clicks aren't used, since there are too few.
  - ~~Users mean different things by the same tier, so the user's own words may matter more than the tier. Technical spec section 4 says a worker gets the tier and a short rule, "never the rule text." In that trip, the coordinator gave the Camden stay the rule "upscale hotel or B&B in Camden," which says the tier again plus a lodging preference, "B&B," that a stay has nowhere else to hold. Other rules only said the tier again in words, such as "meals upscale or posh." So: should a worker get the user's own words with the tier, and where does a stay's lodging preference, such as a B&B, belong?~~ **Partly settled on 2026-10-27 in chat:** a worker gets the user's own words that apply, for budget, meals, and lodging, in place of a tier and a rule. Today a stay has nowhere to hold it, so the coordinator put it in the tier rule, which #184 removes.~~ **Settled on 2026-10-27 in chat:** the trip brief's budget item is replaced by a lodging preferences item, in the user's words, beside meal preferences, and the B&B wish goes there. 233.title: search_near drops places hundreds of miles away

blocks.text: `search_near` sends the worker's query to Google Text Search with a location bias around the stop or stay, not a limit ([tool design](https://github.com/nimbusscale/road-trip-agent/blob/main/design/tools.md) 2.3). That's on purpose: a query that names a farther place, such as "restaurants in Tuolumne Meadows", searches there. But a query about a style, with no place in it, such as "historic bed and breakfast inn Victorian house", can come back with places across the country. Those results are useless, and they cost the worker tokens to read. A search near a stay never needs a place hundreds of miles away.

Adding the town to every query isn't the fix. Around a stay, the best place is often in the next town: in the same session, "lobster pound lobster shack" near Bar Harbor found Trenton Bridge Lobster Pound in Trenton and Beal's Lobster Pier in Southwest Harbor, both about 9 miles out. With "Bar Harbor" in the query, Google would likely rank places in Bar Harbor itself first.

Joe's Bar Harbor session on the live site on 2026-10-30, agent session `89f4dea6-6cb9-4320-a917-c063620acca9`, in the `road-trip-agent` project in Phoenix. Of the 14 `search_near` calls, 6 returned places more than 100 miles away:

- Turn 7, Portland lodging, "historic bed and breakfast inn Victorian house": 6 of 10 results were over 100 miles away, such as B&Bs in St. Augustine, FL, and Sioux Falls, SD, the farthest 2,704 miles.
- Turn 5, Bar Harbor lodging, "retro motel motor court inn": its only result was 1,397 miles away.
- Four more had one or two results 143 to 213 miles away, such as "espresso cafe breakfast" near Portland, and "whale watch cruise" near Bar Harbor in turn 15.
- [Tool design](https://github.com/nimbusscale/road-trip-agent/blob/main/design/tools.md), section 2.3 (`search_near`, and "The near distance biases the search. It doesn't limit it.").
- [Google data source](https://github.com/nimbusscale/road-trip-agent/blob/main/design/data-sources/google.md), the Text Search row for places near a stay.
